## Proof

**Claim:** Yes, the (improper) Riemann integral of $F$ over $[0,\infty)$ equals the Lebesgue integral of $F$ over $(0,\infty)$. Both equal $1$.

**Setup.** We are given $f(x)=e^{-x}$ on $(0,\infty)$ and an extension $F$ of $f$ to $(-\delta,\infty)$ for some $\delta>0$. Hence
$$F(x)=e^{-x}\quad\text{for all }x\in(0,\infty).$$
The value $F(0)$ (and the values on $(-\delta,0]$) are whatever the extension prescribes, but this is irrelevant to both integrals below, since $\{0\}$ has Lebesgue measure $0$ and a single point does not affect a Riemann integral.

**The improper Riemann integral over $[0,\infty)$.** By definition,
$$\int_{0}^{\infty}F(x)\,dx \;=\; \lim_{b\to\infty}\int_{0}^{b}F(x)\,dx.$$
For every $b>0$, $F(x)=e^{-x}$ on $(0,b]$, and the value at the single endpoint $x=0$ does not change the Riemann integral, so
$$\int_{0}^{b}F(x)\,dx \;=\; \int_{0}^{b}e^{-x}\,dx \;=\; \bigl[-e^{-x}\bigr]_{0}^{b} \;=\; 1-e^{-b}.$$
Taking the limit,
$$\int_{0}^{\infty}F(x)\,dx \;=\; \lim_{b\to\infty}(1-e^{-b}) \;=\; 1.$$
The improper Riemann integral converges to $1$.

**The Lebesgue integral over $(0,\infty)$.** On $(0,\infty)$ we have $F(x)=e^{-x}\ge 0$, and $F$ is continuous (hence Borel measurable) there. The Lebesgue integral of a non-negative measurable function is
$$\int_{(0,\infty)}F\,d\mu \;=\; \int_{(0,\infty)}e^{-x}\,d\mu.$$
Since $e^{-x}$ is non-negative, continuous, and Riemann-integrable on every compact subinterval of $(0,\infty)$, the standard theorem relating Riemann and Lebesgue integrals for non-negative continuous functions on intervals gives
$$\int_{(0,\infty)}e^{-x}\,d\mu \;=\; \int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x}\,dx \;=\; 1,$$
where the last equality is the same improper Riemann integral computed above (equivalently, an antiderivative evaluation: $\bigl[-e^{-x}\bigr]_{0}^{\infty}=0-(-1)=1$). Concretely, one may verify this via the monotone convergence theorem applied to $g_{n}(x)=e^{-x}\mathbf{1}_{(0,n]}(x)$, which increases pointwise to $e^{-x}\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}$ and satisfies $\int g_{n}\,d\mu = 1-e^{-n}\to 1$.

**Comparison.**
$$\underbrace{\int_{0}^{\infty}F(x)\,dx}_{\text{improper Riemann on }[0,\infty)} \;=\; 1 \;=\; \underbrace{\int_{(0,\infty)}F\,d\mu}_{\text{Lebesgue on }(0,\infty)}.$$

The two integrals agree. The two apparent sources of discrepancy — the inclusion of the endpoint $0$ in the Riemann domain and the unspecified values of the extension on $(-\delta,0]$ — both concern only the single point $\{0\}$ (and the negative half-line, which lies outside both domains of integration), and a single point has Lebesgue measure $0$ and zero contribution to a Riemann integral. Hence neither can affect the value.

**Conclusion.** The Riemann integral of $F$ over $[0,\infty)$ and the Lebesgue integral of $F$ over $(0,\infty)$ are equal; both are $1$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
